extracted.intended_audience: employers, employment lawyers, policymakers, HR professionals, and public commenters on the FTC non-compete rule
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the FTC's final-rule standards for (1) treating non-competes with senior executives as unfair methods of competition under Section 5, (2) allowing existing senior-executive non-competes to remain in effect, and (3) the two-part definition (compensation threshold + policy-making duties) used to identify "senior executives."

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 5 legal standard for unfair methods of competition
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquiry under section 5 focuses on the nature and tendency of the conduct; the Commission need not make a separate showing of market power or market definition, nor must it show that the conduct directly caused actual harm in the specific instance at issue. The Commission may consider the aggregate effect of conduct, and language about a respondent's size, power, or purpose provides guidance regarding factors the Commission may consider but is not limiting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted guidance: "the Commission need not make a separate showing of market power or market definition. Nor must the Commission show that the conduct directly caused actual harm in the specific instance at issue. Instead, the inquiry under section 5 focuses on the nature and tendency of the conduct. Moreover... the Commission may consider the aggregate effect of conduct as well." Use this standard when assessing whether non-competes constitute an unfair method of competition under section 5 (rather than requiring per se Sherman Act analysis or individualized market-definition proofs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence weighting: enforceability vs use studies and causation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission distinguishes between empirical studies of non-compete 'enforceability' (legal regime changes) and studies of 'use' (observed contractual use) and gives greater weight to enforceability-based analyses for causal findings. Studies that examine use cannot easily differentiate between correlation and causation, so the Commission gives such studies less weight and does not interpret some results causally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Garmaise study (uses legal changes in enforceability) is given significant weight; the Kini, Williams, and Yin study (analyzes use and enforceability together) is given less weight and not interpreted causally. When evaluating empirical evidence, prefer quasi-experimental changes in enforceability to cross-sectional or use-based correlations for causal inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-competes suppress labor mobility and earnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-competes reduce labor mobility and worker earnings across many subgroups (inventors, high-tech workers, low-wage workers, and across the labor force), and this effect also applies to senior executives. Garmaise finds stricter non-compete enforceability reduces within-industry executive mobility by 47% and across-industry executive mobility by 25%; decreased enforceability increases executives' earnings by 12.7% and increases CEOs' earnings growth by 8.2%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: non-competes directly prohibit seeking/accepting other work or starting a business, inhibiting efficient matching and reducing opportunities/earnings. The Commission uses these empirical magnitudes and mechanisms to support the finding that non-competes negatively affect labor markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of buyout clauses is inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibiting buyout clauses in non-competes would not enhance efficiency relative to prohibiting non-competes altogether, because banning buyouts would mean fewer executives could escape their non-competes, reducing labor mobility and efficient matching even further.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implication: Do not adopt a rule that only bans buyout clauses as a substitute for banning non-competes; such a partial approach could exacerbate mobility restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowing existing senior-executive non-competes (limited exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule prohibits entering into or enforcing new non-competes with senior executives (i.e., post-effective-date agreements) but allows existing non-competes with senior executives (entered into before the effective date) to remain in effect based on practical considerations: senior executives are less likely to have been exploited or coerced and are more likely to have bargained for meaningful consideration; rescinding such agreements creates complex, hard-to-value implementation challenges (tax, M&A valuation, clawbacks, litigation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: a limited, easily administrable exception for existing senior-executive non-competes reduces implementation burden while recognizing that negative competitive effects will subside as these non-competes expire. Use this balance of harms and administrability when deciding narrow grandfathering exemptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part definition of 'senior executive' (compensation + job duties)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission defines 'senior executive' using a two-pronged test: (1) the worker was in a policy-making position (job duties test), and (2) the worker received total annual compensation of at least $151,164 in the preceding year (or annualized equivalents under paragraphs (2)(ii) and (2)(iii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraphs clarify annualization for partial-year employment and for departures more than one year before the effective date. The two-part test is modeled on administrable frameworks (e.g., DOL FLSA executive exemption) to capture those most likely to have bargained for meaningful consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation threshold: level and measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: The compensation threshold is $151,164 (based on the 85th percentile of earnings of full-time salaried workers nationally) and applies to 'total annual compensation' in the 'preceding year'; rules define total annual compensation and preceding year and provide annualization rules for part-year employment or prior departures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: a bright-line, objective compensation threshold yields administrability and clarity, reduces uncertainty and in terrorem effects, and minimizes the need for detailed duty-by-duty analysis for workers below the threshold. The Commission declines locality adjustments for this one-time existing-agreement exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Job duties test: 'policy-making position' and its subdefinitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The job duties component requires the worker to have been in a 'policy-making position' as defined in the rule; the final rule includes definitions of 'policy-making position' and related terms ('officer', 'policy-making authority') to identify individuals who exercise the highest levels of authority in an organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: the duties test prevents high-earning workers who lack genuine policy-making authority from qualifying as 'senior executives' and ensures the exception targets individuals likely to have negotiated bespoke agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrability and clarity principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear, objective compensation threshold is essential because it is easily understood by stakeholders, yields administrability benefits, minimizes detailed assessments for most workers, and reduces opportunities for evasion. Exceptions based on vague standards (e.g., 'access to trade secrets' or unspecified 'substantial consideration') would lack clarity and increase compliance costs and litigation risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: avoid exceptions that require case-by-case, fact-intensive inquiry or vague standards that invite evasive employer behavior. Prefer bright-line tests where administrability and predictability are priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of exemption for paid/non-compete consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission declines to adopt an exception for non-competes in exchange for which a worker received compensation because (a) receiving compensation does not mean the worker received fair compensation commensurate with what they'd receive in a competitive market, and (b) such an exception would raise significant administrability issues (e.g., "substantial" or "meaningful" consideration is vague) and could incentivize employers to suppress other compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and risks: bright-line monetary thresholds are unlikely to capture varied financial circumstances; requiring severance equal to salary could induce employers to reduce salary to game the exception; administrability concerns justify relying on the limited senior-executive existing-agreement exemption instead of a general 'paid non-compete' carve-out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of practical impacts (tax, M&A, litigation, clawbacks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rescinding existing non-competes could raise complex practical issues: potential windfalls for workers, uncertainty about returning already-received benefits, tax return amendments, impacts on severance arrangements, clawbacks, disruptions to M&A valuations where non-competes were priced into acquisition deals, and litigation seeking declarations on contract impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These practical implementation concerns support a narrowly administrable exemption for existing senior-executive non-competes to reduce disruption and transition costs while still addressing broader competitive harms over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of bargaining power, exploitation, and coercion in defining exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission frames the senior-executive exception to isolate workers least likely to have experienced exploitation or coercion and most likely to have bargained for meaningful consideration; many highly paid workers without policy-making authority and lower-wage workers with senior titles are excluded because they likely experienced coercion or lacked bargaining power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical and comment record support: the Commission estimates ~0.75% of workers fit the senior-executive definition. Use evidence about bargaining context and exploitation risk when tailoring exceptions to narrow worker groups.
